opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm not a hardcore "Transformers forever" person, but I've been around long enough to see a lot of challengers come and go. Every year or so there's a new architecture that's supposed to replace attention, whether it's some efficient attention variant, state space models, or linear RNNs. Some of them are genuinely interesting ideas. But when you actually scale them up and look at the full picture, Transformers keep holding up really well.

Part of it is that the Transformer is just a very good general-purpose computation substrate. It's simple, it's expressive, and it maps really well onto the hardware we have. Accelerators are basically built to do big matrix multiplies, and the whole ecosystem has co-evolved around that: kernels, compilers, parallelism strategies, inference stacks. So any new architecture isn't just competing with an idea. It's competing with years of engineering and optimization. That's a really high bar.

The second thing is that a lot of the "wins" for alternative architectures show up at small scale or on narrow benchmarks, and then they wash out as you scale. I've worked on efficient Transformers myself, and one lesson I took from that is that inductive biases that help at small scale often don't matter, or even hurt, when you have lots of compute and data. The Transformer's lack of strong assumptions is kind of a feature there.

And third, I think the field has learned that the bigger levers right now are data, training objectives, post-training, and how you use compute at inference time. The architecture is not really the bottleneck. You can get enormous gains without touching the backbone, so there's less pressure to rip it out.

That said, I don't think the Transformer stays frozen. It'll keep evolving. MoE, different attention patterns, hybrids with some recurrent or state-space layers for long context, those kinds of things. In five years it might look pretty different in the details. But I'd bet the core idea, stacked blocks with attention and MLPs trained at scale, is still recognizably there. To really displace it, you'd need something that's clearly better at scale, not just a bit more efficient, and I haven't seen that yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the Transformer will evolve in its details while retaining the core idea of stacked blocks with attention and MLPs, including variants with different attention patterns. This communicates attention as the continuity across architectural changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I get this question a lot, and I think people sometimes expect me to say something like "oh, Transformers are obviously going to be replaced by X." But honestly, my position is kind of the boring one, which is that I don't think the architecture is really the bottleneck anymore.

I spent a good chunk of my time at Google working on architecture research. We did a lot of the "efficient Transformer" stuff, Long Range Arena, all these benchmarks trying to find the thing that would beat vanilla attention. And the recurring lesson, over and over, was that most of these alternatives looked great at small scale and then the gains just evaporated once you scaled up. The Transformer is surprisingly hard to beat when you give it enough data and compute. It's a very good general-purpose inductive bias, or maybe more accurately, a very good lack of inductive bias. It doesn't impose much structure, so it lets the data speak, and that's exactly what you want when you're in the regime where data and compute are abundant.

The other thing is that there's this huge co-evolution between the architecture and the hardware and software stack. TPUs, GPUs, the kernels, the parallelism strategies, FlashAttention, all of this was built around the Transformer. So even if you have an architecture that's, say, ten or twenty percent better in FLOPs on paper, you're fighting against years of systems optimization. The bar for displacing it isn't "slightly better," it's "so much better that it's worth rebuilding the whole stack," and nothing has cleared that bar yet.

I also think people conflate "the Transformer" with the exact 2017 recipe. The thing we call a Transformer today already looks pretty different: RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, grouped query attention, MoE layers. It's been absorbing good ideas the whole time. So when people ask will Transformers persist, I'd say yes, but the Transformer in 2030 will look like a Transformer the same way a modern car looks like a Model T. The skeleton persists because it works, and the improvements get folded in.

And then the last point is just, where is the actual progress coming from right now? It's data, it's scale, it's post-training, it's RL, it's test-time compute. None of that is architecture-bound. If I had a marginal unit of research effort, I would not spend it on replacing attention. I'd spend it on the stuff that's actually moving capabilities. So yeah, I think Transformers persist mostly by default, because nothing has given us a strong enough reason to leave.

r001.rationale: The response says the Transformer’s “skeleton persists” and lists grouped query attention among later additions, but it does not clearly identify continued self-attention as the underlying continuity across variants.

astra-6.text:
I think Transformers will stick around because they’re a very general architecture, and we haven’t really established where their limits are. When something doesn’t work, it’s often hard to tell whether that’s an architectural limitation or whether we need better data, a different training objective, or more compute. So I wouldn’t assume that getting to AGI necessarily requires replacing the Transformer.

There’s also a huge amount of engineering behind making Transformers train and run efficiently. A new architecture has to compete with that whole ecosystem, not just look better in a small experiment. It needs to offer a compelling advantage at scale.

That doesn’t mean nothing changes. We may change the attention mechanism, add memory, or combine Transformers with other components. But I think there’s a plausible path where the overall system becomes much more capable while the Transformer remains a core building block.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the attention mechanism may change, but does not identify continued self-attention as the shared basis across Transformer variants or renamed implementations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Transformer is going to be pretty hard to displace because it’s a very flexible architecture, and we’ve built so much infrastructure around making it scale. If you have a new idea, it’s often easier to incorporate that idea into a Transformer than to replace the whole thing and rebuild the training stack.

And getting to AGI doesn’t necessarily require a fundamentally new architecture. A lot of progress could come from better training objectives, better data, or how we use compute at inference time. Those are all things that can evolve while the underlying model remains a Transformer.

That doesn’t mean attention has to stay exactly as it is today. We might change components or introduce more recurrence or memory. But I would expect an evolution of the architecture rather than a clean break where suddenly everything we’ve built becomes obsolete.

r001.rationale: The response says attention may change and predicts Transformer evolution, but it does not identify continued use of some form of self-attention as the continuity across variants.
